entities.summary:
The Velvet Revolution was a democratization process in Czechoslovakia that took place in 1989. It occurred after years of anti-communist resistance, with key events unfolding in November and December of that year. The revolution was sparked by the growing dissatisfaction of the Czechoslovak population with the communist regime, which was led by General Secretary Miloš Jakeš. The protests were led by a coalition of opposition groups, including Civic Forum, led by Václav Havel, and the Public Against Violence, led by Ján Čarnogurský. The revolution ended with the formation of a new government and the eventual split of Czechoslovakia into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993.

The revolution saw the rise of a new generation of leaders, including Havel, who became the first president of the Czech Republic. The new government implemented free market reforms and established democratic institutions. The Velvet Revolution also led to the end of the Cold War and the eventual collapse of communist regimes across Eastern Europe.

The Velvet Revolution's impact on world history can be seen in its role as a catalyst for the collapse of the Soviet Empire and the end of the Cold War. It paved the way for the reunification of Germany and the spread of democracy across Eastern Europe. The revolution also had a lasting impact on the global balance of power and continues to shape international relations today.

The Velvet Revolution remains a powerful symbol of the power of peaceful resistance and the importance of protecting human rights and democracy. As Václav Havel once said, 'The Velvet Revolution was not just a revolution, but a revolution of the heart.'
